title: THE PERSON WHO BROKE YOU MAY NEVER APOLOGIZE. DOES GOD STILL EXPECT YOU TO FORGIVE?
paragraphs: THE PERSON WHO BROKE YOU MAY NEVER APOLOGIZE. DOES GOD STILL EXPECT YOU TO FORGIVE?
“Do Not Repay Anyone Evil for Evil” — The Terrifying Truth About Revenge, the Justice God Never Forgets, and the Freedom Jesus Offers to Those Who Have Been Wronged.
There is a kind of pain that doesn't make you cry anymore.
It makes you quiet.
You still go to work. You still answer messages. You still smile when someone asks how you're doing. You may even sit in church, lift your hands during worship, and whisper, “Thank You, Jesus.”
But somewhere beneath that smile, there is a conversation you keep replaying.
Something they said.
Something they did.
The moment you realized someone you trusted was capable of hurting you that deeply.
And sometimes, when the house is quiet and nobody is watching, you imagine what it would feel like if they finally experienced what they put you through.
Not because you believe you're a cruel person.
But because you're tired of being the one who suffers while they seem to walk away untouched.
You want them to understand.
You want the truth to come out.
You want somebody to look at what happened and finally say, “What they did to you was wrong.”
And perhaps the hardest part is that you have prayed about it.
More than once.
You have asked God to heal your heart. You have tried to forgive. You have told yourself that you're moving forward.
But then you see their name.
You hear someone praise their character.
You discover they're doing well.
And suddenly, the wound you thought was healing starts bleeding again.
Then you encounter a command from Scripture that almost feels impossible.
“Recompense to no man evil for evil.” — Romans 12:17, KJV
And something inside you wants to ask God a question you would never dare ask out loud.
Lord, do You understand what they did to me?
Because it is one thing to preach forgiveness when you have never been betrayed.
It is another thing to obey Jesus when the person who wounded you is still denying the wound exists.
But what if this command is not God dismissing your pain?
What if it is God refusing to let the person who hurt you become the master of your heart?
And what if the justice you have been begging for is far more serious, far more holy, and far more complete than anything revenge could ever accomplish?
Stay with this truth, because before we reach the cross, we need to confront something uncomfortable.
Sometimes the person we most desperately want God to punish is the person whose approval we once desperately wanted.
And that is why revenge can feel so personal.
It is not always hatred.
Sometimes it is grief wearing armor.
Sometimes it is humiliation demanding a witness.
Sometimes it is the desperate desire to recover the dignity someone tried to take away.
But Scripture does not allow our pain to become permission to sin.
Paul writes in Romans 12:17:
Transliterated: Mēdeni kakon anti kakou apodidontes.
The Greek expression means, in context, “Repaying no one evil in exchange for evil.”
Notice the word ἀποδιδόντες (apodidontes), from apodidōmi, a verb that can mean to give back, return, repay, or render what is due.
Paul is addressing the impulse to return an injury in kind.
Someone humiliates you, so you humiliate them.
Someone spreads lies about you, so you spread lies about them.
Someone betrays your confidence, so you expose their secrets.
Someone wounds your reputation, so you dedicate yourself to destroying theirs.
The world may call that getting even.
Scripture calls us to something different.
But we must understand what Paul is actually commanding.
He is not saying evil is harmless.
He is not saying injustice should be ignored.
He is not telling victims to remain in dangerous situations.
And he is certainly not teaching that a Christian must surrender the right to seek protection, report abuse, tell the truth, establish boundaries, or pursue lawful justice.
Refusing revenge is not the same as refusing justice.
That distinction matters.
Especially to the woman who has been manipulated into believing that forgiving an abusive husband means returning to danger.
Especially to the child who was told to stay silent because exposing a respected adult would embarrass the family.
Especially to the employee whose integrity was attacked by someone with greater influence.
Especially to the believer whose church experience left wounds that nobody wanted to acknowledge.
The Gospel does not require you to call darkness light.
Jesus never taught that holiness means pretending evil did not happen.
In fact, Romans 12 must be read alongside Romans 13, where Paul describes governing authority as having a responsibility to restrain wrongdoing and administer justice.
The same apostle who forbids personal vengeance recognizes a legitimate place for public justice.
That means you can forgive someone and still tell the truth.
You can release hatred and still pursue accountability.
You can pray for someone's repentance and still refuse to trust them with access to your life.
You can desire their salvation and still testify honestly about what they did.
And if someone has harmed you or another person, seeking safety and appropriate help is not a failure of Christian forgiveness.
It may be an essential act of wisdom, truth, and love.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust.
Reconciliation requires more than one person's willingness. Where there has been serious wrongdoing, repentance, changed conduct, and appropriate safeguards matter.
God does not ask you to pretend that broken trust was never broken.
But He does ask you to surrender something.
And this is where the command becomes deeply personal.
Because sometimes, after every necessary boundary has been established and every appropriate avenue of justice has been pursued, something remains.
The private courtroom inside your heart.
The place where you prosecute the same person every night.
The place where you imagine the perfect confrontation.
The place where you rehearse what you should have said.
The place where you secretly hope their life falls apart so yours will finally feel vindicated.
That is the courtroom God wants to enter.
Not to declare the guilty innocent.
But to free you from the burden of trying to become the final judge.
Paul continues:
“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.” — Romans 12:19, KJV
The Greek includes this declaration:
“Ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις, ἐγὼ ἀνταποδώσω.”
Emoi ekdikēsis, egō antapodōsō.
“Vengeance belongs to Me; I will repay.”
Paul is drawing from Deuteronomy 32:35, where the Hebrew text begins:
“לִי נָקָם וְשִׁלֵּם”
Li naqam veshillem.
A close rendering is, “Vengeance is Mine, and recompense.”
The Hebrew word נָקָם (naqam) refers to vengeance or retribution. In this biblical setting, the declaration establishes God's authority over final repayment and judgment.
That matters because human revenge and divine justice are not interchangeable.
Our judgment is limited.
Our motives are mixed.
Our knowledge is incomplete.
Even when we have been genuinely wronged, anger can distort what we believe justice requires.
But God sees what we cannot.
He sees the deed.
He sees the motive.
He sees the concealed evidence.
He sees the tears no one believed.
He sees the private cruelty behind the public reputation.
And He sees the sin we ourselves are tempted to commit in response.
Nothing is hidden from Him.
Yet this does not mean God promises that every offender will suffer an obvious downfall during our lifetime.
Scripture does not give us permission to predict how or when divine judgment will appear.
Some wrongs are exposed publicly.
Others remain hidden until the final judgment.
Some offenders repent and receive mercy through Christ.
Others persist in rebellion and face God's righteous judgment.
But no evil is beyond His knowledge.
And no sinner is beyond His power to call to repentance.
When God says vengeance belongs to Him, He is not promising to satisfy every desire for retaliation. He is declaring that ultimate justice belongs to His holiness, not our wounded pride.
That truth is both comforting and terrifying.
Comforting, because the victim is not forgotten.
Terrifying, because it means we cannot demand justice for someone else's sin while treating our own sin as insignificant.
Think about Joseph.
His brothers stripped him of his robe, threw him into a pit, and sold him into slavery.
They took years from his life.
They shattered his father's heart.
They betrayed someone who had every reason to expect loyalty from them.
And when Joseph eventually held power over the very men who had betrayed him, he possessed an opportunity most wounded people can only imagine.
He could make them pay.
He could humiliate them.
He could imprison them.
He could turn their helplessness into his satisfaction.
But after their father's death, when his brothers feared retaliation, Joseph answered:
“Fear not: for am I in the place of God?” — Genesis 50:19, KJV
Read that again.
Am I in the place of God?
Joseph did not deny their evil.
In the very next verse, he said:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.” — Genesis 50:20, KJV
Their intention was evil.
Joseph called it evil.
He did not rename betrayal as a blessing.
He did not excuse their actions because God had brought good out of his suffering.
He recognized that God's providence was greater than their wicked intentions.
This is one of the most important distinctions in Christian healing.
God bringing good out of evil does not make the evil good.
The betrayal was still betrayal.
The pit was still a pit.
The slavery was still injustice.
But the brothers' sin did not have the final authority to define Joseph's future.
And perhaps that is the word someone reading this desperately needs.
What happened to you may have changed your life.
It may have cost you years.
It may have damaged relationships, opportunities, finances, or your ability to trust.
You may still be dealing with consequences that the person responsible never has to see.
But their wrongdoing does not possess ultimate authority over who you are in Christ.
Your pain is real.
Your loss matters.
And your story is not finished simply because someone else tried to write a cruel chapter.
There is another story, however, that brings us even closer to the heart of the Gospel.
A man named Stephen.
He was not being misunderstood in an ordinary disagreement.
He was being killed.
In Acts 7, Stephen was dragged into a violent confrontation, and the crowd stoned him.
As his life was being taken, he cried out:
“Lord, lay not this sin to their charge.” — Acts 7:60, KJV
Stephen did not call their actions righteous.
He called them sin.
Yet he prayed for mercy.
And standing nearby was a young man named Saul, who approved of Stephen's death, as Acts 8:1 records.
Think about that.
One of the people associated with the persecution of the early church would later become the apostle Paul.
The man who would write, “Recompense to no man evil for evil.”
The man who would write, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
The man who would write about overcoming evil with good.
Paul knew something about both sides of human cruelty.
He had participated in persecution.
And later, for the sake of Christ, he endured persecution himself.
We cannot claim Scripture explicitly says Stephen's prayer caused Saul's conversion.
It does not.
But the connection is still astonishing.
A persecutor became a preacher of the grace he once opposed.
A man associated with the suffering of believers became a servant of the Christ those believers worshiped.
And this confronts us with a difficult Gospel question.
What if the person you want destroyed is someone God may yet bring to repentance?
That possibility does not erase accountability.
It does not mean you must remain in their life.
It does not mean they deserve immediate access to your trust.
But it does mean the mercy of God is not limited by our inability to imagine someone's transformation.
And if that thought makes you uncomfortable, consider how deeply we ourselves depend on that same mercy.
Because the Gospel is not the story of innocent people learning to tolerate guilty people.
It is the story of guilty people being offered reconciliation with a holy God through Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we had proven ourselves worthy.
Not after we had made enough promises to compensate for our failures.
Christ died for us while we were sinners.
And here, at the cross, every shallow explanation of forgiveness falls apart.
Because God did not simply overlook evil.
He did not declare sin unimportant.
He did not abandon justice to make mercy possible.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, willingly gave Himself for sinners.
As Isaiah 53:5 declares:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.” — KJV
And as 1 Peter 2:24 teaches, Christ bore our sins in His own body on the tree.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the greatness of divine love.
God's grace is not cheap because Christ's sacrifice was not cheap.
And when Jesus was crucified, He did something that should stop every revenge-driven heart in its tracks.
Luke 23:34 records His prayer:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” — KJV

Some early manuscripts of Luke omit this sentence, while many others preserve it. The prayer is part of the traditional text of Luke and is consistent with Jesus' teaching to love enemies and pray for persecutors.
Consider the scene.
He was mocked.
Stripped.
Falsely accused.
Beaten.
Nailed to a cross.
The One who had never sinned was suffering under the cruelty of sinful people.
And He prayed for forgiveness.
This was not weakness.
Jesus was not powerless.
He was willingly accomplishing the Father's redemptive purpose.
And His mercy did not mean that everyone who participated in His crucifixion was automatically forgiven without repentance and faith.
The New Testament continues to call sinners to repent and believe in Christ.
But the prayer reveals the heart of the Savior.
Even while suffering injustice, Jesus was not consumed by the desire for personal retaliation.
Now think about your own heart.
Not to minimize what happened to you.
Not to compare your suffering with someone else's.
But to ask a question that reaches beneath the anger.
If Jesus has shown me mercy I could never earn, what would it look like for that mercy to begin changing the way I respond to those who have wronged me?
This is where forgiveness becomes more than an inspirational quotation.
It becomes discipleship.
And discipleship can hurt.
Because forgiving someone may mean surrendering the fantasy of seeing them humiliated.
It may mean refusing to recruit others into a campaign of personal destruction.
It may mean stopping yourself from repeating a story when your real purpose is no longer truth or protection, but punishment.
It may mean praying, through clenched teeth, “Lord, I want justice, but I do not want to become unjust.”
It may mean admitting that you have started loving the thought of their downfall more than you love your own obedience to Christ.
And perhaps that is the confession you have been avoiding.
You do not merely want them to understand your pain.
Part of you wants them to feel it.
You want the phone call.
The exposed secret.
The public embarrassment.
The moment when everyone finally sees them the way you do.
You imagine that day will bring peace.
But revenge cannot heal the deepest injury of betrayal.
Even if an offender experiences consequences, you may still need to grieve, rebuild, and learn to trust wisely again.
Their suffering cannot return every lost year.
Their embarrassment cannot automatically restore your sense of safety.
Their apology, if it ever comes, cannot become the foundation of your identity.
Only Christ can be that foundation.
And He invites you to something better than being permanently defined by the person who hurt you.
Paul writes:
In Greek:
“Μὴ νικῶ ὑπὸ τοῦ κακοῦ, ἀλλὰ νίκα ἐν τῷ ἀγαθῷ τὸ κακόν.”
Mē nikō hypo tou kakou, alla nika en tō agathō to kakon.
A close rendering is: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”
The language of overcoming is striking.
Paul does not present Christian goodness as surrender to evil.
He presents it as a form of victory over evil.
Not victory through cruelty.
Not victory through deception.
Not victory through becoming a mirror image of the offender.
But victory through conduct shaped by the goodness of God.
And sometimes that goodness looks surprisingly ordinary.
It looks like refusing to lie, even when lying would damage the person who lied about you.
It looks like telling the truth without exaggeration.
It looks like seeking help before anger turns into violence.
It looks like refusing to expose private information merely to humiliate someone.
It looks like reporting wrongdoing through appropriate channels, even when others pressure you to remain silent.
It looks like protecting vulnerable people.
It looks like praying for an enemy's repentance while also accepting that trust must be rebuilt through evidence, not words alone.
It looks like choosing not to let another person's sin determine your own character.
And sometimes it looks like doing something almost nobody notices.
You put down your phone.
You delete the cruel response you were about to send.
You refuse to publish the post designed to destroy someone's reputation.
You sit quietly before God and say:
“Jesus, I am still angry.”
Not a polished prayer.
Not a religious performance.
Just the truth.

“I still remember what happened. I still want them to admit it. I still feel sick when I think about it. I don't know how to forgive them completely. But I don't want this bitterness to become who I am. Please help me.”
That prayer may not remove the pain immediately.
Forgiveness can be a deliberate act of obedience, and the emotional healing associated with it may unfold over time.
Some wounds require wise pastoral care, trusted community, counseling, and practical protection.
There is no biblical requirement to pretend healing is instant.
But there is an invitation to begin.
To bring your anger into the presence of God rather than allowing it to rule you.
To entrust final judgment to Him while taking whatever truthful, lawful, and wise steps are needed.
To refuse to let hatred become the inheritance you carry into every future relationship.
And to remember that you are not being asked to do this through sheer willpower.
The Holy Spirit works in believers to produce love, patience, kindness, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).
This is not simply self-improvement.
It is the transforming work of God in a surrendered life.
And that brings us to a question more important than whether the person who hurt you will ever apologize.
Who are you becoming while you wait?
Are you becoming more truthful?
More prayerful?
More courageous?
More compassionate toward others who suffer?
More dependent on Christ?
Or is the injury slowly teaching you to become someone you never wanted to be?
There is no shame in admitting that bitterness has taken root.
But there is danger in protecting it.
Hebrews 12:15 warns about a root of bitterness that can spring up and cause trouble, defiling many.
Bitterness rarely announces itself as bitterness.
Sometimes it sounds like, “I'm just being realistic.”
Sometimes it sounds like, “I will never trust anyone again.”
Sometimes it sounds like, “People deserve whatever happens to them.”
And sometimes it sounds like, “I know God says to forgive, but He cannot possibly expect that from me.”
Yet Jesus does not call us to forgive because the offender deserves our mercy.
He calls us to forgive as people who have received mercy from Him.
Ephesians 4:32 says:
“And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.” — KJV
The standard is not the offender's worthiness.
The pattern is God's grace in Christ.
And that is where the story changes.
Not because the scandal was imaginary.
Not because the damage did not matter.
Not because consequences should disappear.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem people whose lives have been marked by the sins of others and by their own sinful responses.
He can restore what bitterness has eroded.
He can teach a wounded heart to love without becoming naive.
He can teach a fearful person to establish boundaries without surrendering to hatred.
He can teach a betrayed believer to seek justice without worshiping revenge.
He can teach us to tell the truth without becoming cruel.
And most astonishingly, He can save the guilty who repent and place their faith in Him.
That is the scandal of grace.
It is available to the wounded sinner.
And it is available to the sinner who wounded someone else.
Not as permission to continue in evil.
But as an invitation to repentance, forgiveness, and a transformed life.
Maybe you are reading this as the person who was betrayed.
But maybe you are reading it as the person who did the betraying.
You know what you said.
You know what you concealed.
You know whose trust you violated.
You have justified it for years because admitting the truth would require you to confront the damage.
If that is you, do not use this article to demand forgiveness from the person you hurt.
Do not weaponize Romans 12 against someone who is still suffering from your actions.
Do not tell them they are bitter because they have boundaries.
Instead, repent.
Confess your sin to God.
Tell the truth where appropriate.
Accept responsibility.
Make restitution where possible.
Submit to necessary accountability and lawful consequences.
And understand that another person's forgiveness does not entitle you to immediate reconciliation.
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace calls us to turn away from sin and toward Jesus Christ.
And if you are the one who has been wronged, hear this carefully.
You are allowed to grieve.
You are allowed to acknowledge that something was stolen from you.
You are allowed to seek justice.
You are allowed to say no.
You are allowed to protect yourself and those entrusted to your care.
But you do not have to build your entire future around the moment someone betrayed you.
The person who hurt you may never apologize.
They may never confess.
They may never fully understand what their actions cost.
They may even continue telling a version of the story in which they are the victim.
But their refusal to repent does not prevent you from drawing near to Jesus.
And their refusal to change does not have to determine whether you obey Him.
There is a freedom in saying:

“Lord, I will not call evil good. I will not abandon truth. I will not refuse necessary justice. But I surrender my desire to personally destroy the one who hurt me. Judge rightly. Protect the vulnerable. Bring repentance where You will. And keep my heart from becoming captive to hatred.”
That is not a small prayer.
That is spiritual warfare against the bitterness that wants to take possession of your life.
That is a wounded disciple choosing to follow a crucified and risen Savior.
And perhaps, tonight, that is where your healing begins.
Not with an apology.
Not with a dramatic public vindication.
Not with the downfall of the person who wronged you.
But with a quiet surrender before the Lord who knows every detail.
You may be surprised how many people have been carrying the same struggle in silence.
Not to glorify the person who hurt you, but to testify to the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
Someone reading your words may be standing at the very point where you once stood.
Angry.
Exhausted.
Tempted to retaliate.
Wondering whether obedience to Jesus is even possible after such a deep betrayal.
Your testimony could remind them that God's grace is sufficient for the next faithful step.
And perhaps there is someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this message more than you realize.
Because there may come another night when the anger returns.
Another moment when an old memory rises.
Another day when you are tempted to repay evil with evil.
And on that day, you may need to return to these words:
“Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.” — Romans 12:21
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to publish words that stir emotions for a few minutes.
But to keep pointing people back to the living Word of God, to repentance, to biblical truth, to the cross, and to the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.

If this ministry has encouraged you, challenged you, or helped you understand Scripture more deeply, consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, fellow believers, seekers, and even those who have grown distant from faith to follow as well.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, not under compulsion.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
And Philippians 4:15–18 provides a beautiful example of believers voluntarily supporting Gospel ministry.

Supporting faithful Christian work can glorify God when it is done with sincere motives and wise stewardship. But your generosity should never be driven by guilt, fear, or the suggestion that God's love can be purchased.
If you already faithfully support your local church, your family, or people in need, please continue to take those responsibilities seriously.
It is participating in a ministry that seeks to keep Jesus Christ at the center of the conversation.

These resources are intended to help readers study Scripture, develop a stronger prayer life, understand Christian doctrine, pursue spiritual maturity, and continue walking with the Lord beyond a single article.
Because the goal is not simply to grow an audience.
It is to see people come to know Jesus, believers become rooted in His Word, wounded hearts receive wise and compassionate care, and lives be transformed through repentance and faith.
Before you leave, I want to return to the question that may have brought you here.
What happens when someone does evil to you and gets away with it?
The answer is not that evil stops mattering.
The answer is not that Christians must become passive.
The answer is not that God promises immediate punishment on demand.
The answer is that Jesus calls His people to entrust final vengeance to the righteous Judge, pursue what is right, and refuse to let evil reproduce itself in their own hearts.
And we know this command is not empty because of the cross.
At Calvary, God demonstrated that He takes sin seriously enough to judge it and loves sinners enough to provide a Savior.
At the empty tomb, He demonstrated that evil and death do not have the final word.
The risen Christ is not indifferent to injustice.
He is the Lord before whom every life will ultimately be accountable.
And He is the Savior who offers forgiveness and new life to everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith.
So tonight, if you are still carrying the weight of what someone did, you can bring it to Him.
You do not have to invent a beautiful prayer.
You can simply say:
“Jesus, You know what happened.
You know what I lost.
You know how angry I have been.
You know the things I have imagined doing in return.
Forgive me for the sinful desires I have allowed to grow in my heart.
Give me courage to pursue truth and justice without hatred.
Give me wisdom to establish the boundaries I need.
Protect those who are vulnerable.
Lead those who have done wrong to genuine repentance.
And where my heart is still wounded, teach me to trust You.
I surrender the final judgment to You.
Not because what happened was acceptable.
But because You are righteous, and I am not God.
Heal what bitterness has damaged.
Restore what You desire to restore.
And make me more like Jesus.
Amen.”
Maybe tomorrow you will still remember.
Maybe the ache will still be there.
Maybe the person who hurt you will continue living as though nothing happened.
But you can still choose the next faithful step.
You can refuse the cruel message.
You can speak the truth.
You can seek help.
You can pray.
You can forgive without pretending.
You can pursue justice without becoming vengeful.
And you can trust that the God who raised Jesus Christ from the dead is able to sustain you even through the chapters you never wanted to live.
Because the greatest victory is not watching your enemy become miserable.
It is becoming more like Christ without allowing your enemy's sin to become your own.
They may never give you the apology you deserved, but you do not have to give their wrongdoing the rest of your life.
